pronunciation.approximation: 'suh-MUN-tuh-bhud-ruh' — the bh is aspirated like 'b-hud' in one breath; the name runs even and calm, like the practice it names.
pronunciation.note: Samantabhadra is samanta, 'on all sides, universal,' + bhadra, 'good, auspicious' (Monier-Williams) — 'Universal Good.' Tier 2 by rule: the owned restoration 'Samantabhadra' preserves nothing that plain ASCII 'samantabhadra' loses — no diacritics, no distinctive atomic letters. The name's distinction is lexical, not orthographic: it means the good that has no edges.

domains.title: Samantabhadra
domains.subtitle: Universal Good
domains.lead: Samantabhadra is the bodhisattva of practice: if Mañjuśrī wields the sword of wisdom, Samantabhadra is the goodness that actually walks — his ten great vows (homage, offering, confession, rejoicing, dedication...) are the Mahāyāna's complete curriculum of the heart, recited daily from Wutai to Lhasa.

cards.name: The Ten Great Vows
cards.desc: Homage, praise, offering, confession, rejoicing, requesting the teaching, beseeching buddhas to remain, imitation, dedication, transfer — the Avataṃsaka's whole practice in ten lines.

cards.name: The Six-Tusked White Elephant
cards.desc: His mount, fragrant and steadfast: practice that carries all beings without hurry or display.

cards.name: The King of Prayers
cards.desc: The Bhadracarī-praṇidhāna — 'Vows of Good Conduct' — closing the Avataṃsaka and opening every Tibetan monastery's day.

cards.name: Mount Emei's Patron
cards.desc: Pǔxián's earthly seat, one of China's four sacred Buddhist mountains — where his bronze elephant has stood since 980 CE.

mythology.lead: Samantabhadra's mythology is the biography of goodness as a discipline. He closes the two greatest Mahāyāna sūtras with vows rather than visions, becomes Tibet's primordial Buddha without ever leaving his elephant, and turns a Sichuan peak into the most walked bodhimaṇḍa in China. His stories are quiet — and deliberately so.

myths.title: The Ten Great Vows
myths.text: The Avataṃsaka Sūtra closes with his testament, the Bhadracarī-praṇidhāna or Vows of Good Conduct: homage to all buddhas as numerous as atoms, praise of their virtues, offerings as vast as space, confession of faults, rejoicing in others' merit, requesting the wheel of Dharma be turned, beseeching buddhas not to pass into nirvāṇa, constant imitation of their deeds, dedication of all merit, and its transfer to all beings — whatever good I have done, may all beings share it. The prayer is appended to the great sūtra in its Chinese recensions and has never left the tradition's daily life: Tibetan monasteries chant it at the close of every session, and East Asian liturgy still folds its verses into repentance rites. Ten lines carry the entire Mahāyāna practice — the myth's point is that goodness, fully articulated, turns out to be this short and this inexhaustible.

myths.title: The Vow of the Lotus
myths.text: The Lotus Sūtra ends not with the Buddha but with a visitor. Its twenty-eighth chapter brings Samantabhadra from the eastern land, riding a great white elephant with six tusks, each tusk bearing seven lotuses, each lotus a radiant Buddha, surrounded by an entourage streaming across the sky — and he vows before the assembly to protect anyone who keeps, reads, or teaches the Lotus in the latter age, sending his fragrant elephant and his retinue to guard them, even laying his hand on their heads in blessing. To forgetful minds he grants dhāraṇīs — spells of retention — so the sūtra survives its readers. The closing chapter is the sūtra handing itself to practice: wisdom (the Lotus's teaching) sealed by goodness (the bodhisattva who promises to carry it). A scripture that ends in a vow is telling you how it intends to be read — not admired, but kept.

myths.title: The Primordial Buddha of Tibet
myths.text: In Tibet's oldest school, the Nyingma, Samantabhadra rose from bodhisattva to ground of being. Kun tu bzang po — the All-Good One — is the dharmakāya itself, the primordial Buddha who never entered samsara because there was nothing to enter: blue, naked, without ornaments of any kind, seated in equipoise with his consort Kun tu bzang mo in the gesture of the mind's own nature. The Kunjed Gyalpo, the 'All-Creating King' tantra, gives him the leading voice: the whole of reality, the tantra says, is the display of his mind, and awakening is not something attained but something remembered. Doctrinally this is a world away from the elephant-riding vow-maker of the Lotus Sūtra — yet the tradition holds both without strain, for the myth's meaning is the same in both registers: goodness is not a virtue acquired but the original condition nothing can add to or subtract from.

myths.title: The Elephant on the Golden Summit
myths.text: China's geography made him its most walked mountain. Pǔxián's bodhimaṇḍa is Éméi shān, the lofty 'Eyebrow' peak of Sichuan — one of the four sacred Buddhist mountains, where the founding legend (recorded in the mountain's gazetteers) tells of a white elephant seen on the heights in the Eastern Han, and of a temple raised where it stood. The mountain's great relic is the Wannian Temple bronze: an elephant bearing Pǔxián, cast in 980 CE under the Song emperor Taizu — over seven meters tall and some sixty-two tonnes, still standing where its mould was poured. Pilgrims climbing the 'seas of clouds' to the Golden Summit report the bodhisattva's apparition in the mountain's famous halo of light, his elephant's outline swimming in the spectral sun. The myth gives practice a landscape you can climb: vows at the bottom, good at the top, and the mountain itself unable to tell the difference.

lore.syncretism: Across East Asia he is the third of the great bodhisattva triad — with Avalokiteśvara (compassion) and Mañjuśrī (wisdom) — the trio enthroned beside Śākyamuni in countless Chinese halls: the heart, the head, and the hands. Japan received Fugen with the same triad logic, and medieval honji-suijaku thought read him as the Buddhist truth behind several kami. Tibet's reception was the boldest: the Nyingma school made Kun tu bzang po the primordial Buddha, the dharmakāya personified, so that the bodhisattva of good conduct became the very ground of enlightenment — practice revealed as the nature of mind itself. The two identities never merged, and the tradition sees no contradiction: the elephant-rider is what the All-Good One looks like when he consents to have a form.
lore.culturalLegacy: Samantabhadra's legacy is the most recited prayer in the Mahāyāna world: the Bhadracarī, his ten vows, closes the day's practice in monasteries from Dharamsala to Kyoto, and its verses — just as Samantabhadra practiced, so may I — are the template of Buddhist dedication across Asia. Mount Emei, his seat, is a UNESCO-listed sacred landscape climbed by pilgrims for two thousand years, its ten-thousand-year temple guarding his bronze elephant. In Japan, Fugen presides over the Lotus Sūtra's protection cult; in Tibet, Kun tu bzang po opens the Dzogchen teachings as the name of the mind's own nature. The restoration Samantabhadra needs no diacritics to carry its meaning — the name itself is the sentence: good, on all sides, without exception.
lore.extendedMeditation: Samantabhadra is the answer to the suspicion that the Mahāyāna is all vision and no work. The Avataṃsaka gives us a cosmos of jeweled interpenetration — and then, in its final pages, hands the whole thing to a bodhisattva on an elephant and ten vows. The placement is the teaching: contemplation without practice is a postcard; practice is the journey the postcard describes. His vows are famously unglamorous — homage, praise, offering, confession, rejoicing — none of them beyond a beginner, all of them infinite. That combination is the point: a practice anyone can start and no one can finish is precisely the shape of a life. He is also the bodhisattva of the collective: every vow ends in dedication, the merit poured back into the common account. If Mañjuśrī asks what you know, Samantabhadra asks what you did with it — and his elephant does not hurry, because goodness, unlike insight, is allowed to take forever.

lore.archaeology: His bronze at Wannian Temple on Mount Emei — Pǔxián riding an elephant, cast 980 CE under Song Taizu, some sixty-two tonnes of it — is among the largest and oldest surviving bronze Buddhist images in China, and the temple's founding legend reaches back to a Han-era sighting on the same slopes. The mountain's Golden Summit temples, rebuilt through the centuries, still anchor a living pilgrimage. At Dunhuang, ninth- and tenth-century mural fragments and banner paintings of the Avataṃsaka's assemblies preserve his early iconography, and the Tibetan manuscript caches of the same caves include early copies of the Kunjed Gyalpo — the primordial Buddha's text traveling the Silk Road in his name.
